title: The Crisp Dollar Bill Myth, and Everything Else Travelers Get Wrong About Paying in Cambodia
summary: Torn dollars, riel change, ATM runs: most advice about money in Cambodia is outdated. Here is what paying with KHQR actually looks like, and how visitors can join in without a local bank.
body_markdown:
Ask around before a trip to Cambodia and you will collect the same warnings every traveler has heard for twenty years. Bring US dollars, but only perfect ones. Expect your change in a mystery currency. Carry small bills or suffer. Some of that advice was true once. Most of it is now a way to make your trip harder than it needs to be, because in 2026 Cambodia runs on a national QR system that is arguably ahead of what many visitors have back home. Let's take the common beliefs one at a time.


## Myth: Cambodia is cash country, so stock up on pristine dollar bills


This is the big one, and it is the most out of date. Yes, US dollars circulate alongside the Cambodian riel, and yes, merchants have historically rejected notes with tears, ink marks, or heavy creases. Travelers used to stand at the bank counter at home inspecting twenties like diamond dealers.


Here is what actually happened in Cambodia while that advice kept circulating: the National Bank of Cambodia built Bakong, a payment backbone that links banks and wallets across the country, and standardized a single QR format called KHQR. That red KHQR sticker is now on the glass at coffee chains in Phnom Penh, taped to the noodle cart outside, laminated and hanging from the tuk-tuk driver's mirror, and pinned next to the cash tray at the pharmacy. Locals scan it dozens of times a day. When you pay by KHQR, nobody inspects your banknotes, because there are no banknotes.


## Myth: the dual currency thing means constant mental math


Cambodia's two-currency habit genuinely confuses visitors. Prices at restaurants and hotels are often quoted in dollars. Small purchases, market stalls, and anything under about a dollar tend to live in riel. Pay cash and you get a hybrid outcome: hand over dollars, receive change as a small stack of riel notes you now have to value on the fly, then spend before you leave the country, because riel is not much use anywhere else.


QR payments dissolve this problem almost completely. The merchant enters the amount, you see it on your screen, you confirm, done. The exact sum moves, in the currency the merchant priced it in. No change, no riel accumulating in your pocket like ballast, no pausing mid-transaction to divide by thousands. With Moreta Pay specifically, you also see the FX conversion from your home currency before you confirm, so the question of "what did that actually cost me" is answered on the spot rather than on your card statement weeks later.


## Myth: KHQR is for locals with Cambodian bank accounts


This one is half true, and it is the half-truth that strands most visitors. Bakong wallets and the local banking apps that generate and scan KHQR codes generally require a Cambodian account or local onboarding, which is a paperwork wall for someone on a thirty-day visa or even a yearlong remote-work stint.


But the merchant side does not care where your money comes from. The code on the counter is a standard KHQR code, and any app that can speak it can pay it. That is exactly the gap Moreta Pay fills: you connect your home bank (US via Plaid or ACH, European SEPA, UK Faster Payments, Canadian e-Transfer) or an international card, top up a wallet in your own currency, and then scan the same red code the local in front of you just scanned. Scan, check the merchant name and amount, confirm. The merchant is paid instantly in their currency, and you never opened a Cambodian account or stood in a bank branch with your passport.


## Myth: QR only works in Phnom Penh


Phnom Penh is saturated, true. But KHQR adoption spread fast precisely because it is a single national standard rather than a patchwork of competing wallets. In Siem Reap, the cafes and massage shops near Pub Street take it, and so do plenty of stalls in the old market. Kampot's riverside guesthouses and pepper-farm tour operators have the sticker. Battambang's coffee shops do too. Even in smaller provincial towns, any business that banks with a Cambodian bank tends to have a code, because for the merchant it is free, instant, and safer than a drawer of mixed dollars and riel.


Should you carry zero cash? Keep a little riel for rural ferry crossings, remote temple donations, and the occasional vendor whose phone battery died. But "a little riel as backup" is a very different trip from "a money belt of inspected twenties."


## Myth: the ATM is still your most practical option


Cambodian ATMs will happily serve a foreign card, and they will just as happily layer on operator fees, your home bank's foreign transaction fees, and a withdrawal that arrives as large US bills. Which puts you right back at myth number two: the street vendor cannot break a fifty, so you overbuy or walk away, and every purchase becomes a small-change negotiation. The ATM does not solve Cambodia's money friction, it manufactures more of it. Topping up a wallet from your own bank in your own currency, then paying exact amounts by QR, skips the entire cycle.


## Myth: booking and paying online still needs a local card


Cambodia's QR ecosystem is not limited to physical counters. Plenty of online checkouts in the region, including platforms travelers actually use like Agoda and Trip.com, offer QR-based payment at checkout. You are shown a code on screen, you scan it with your phone instead of typing card numbers into a form, and the payment clears the same way it does at the noodle stall. For anyone settling in longer, bill payments in supported countries work through the same scan-and-confirm flow, which matters once you have a Phnom Penh apartment with an electricity bill.


## Myth: every Southeast Asian country needs its own payment setup


Travelers often assume that whatever they figure out for Cambodia resets at the border. It does not have to. The region has largely converged on national QR standards, and one wallet that speaks them saves you relearning the system every few weeks. If Cambodia is one stop on a longer loop, the same approach carries you through


[Thailand's PromptPay network](https://moretapay.com/blog/thailand-promptpay-qr-payments-how-to-pay-like-a-local-no-cash-2026-2026-10-03)

[paying in kip without a Lao bank](https://moretapay.com/blog/laos-expat-daily-payments-lao-qr-kip-no-bank-account-2026-2026-09-28)

## What to actually do before you land


Skip the ritual of hunting for flawless banknotes. Install Moreta Pay, connect your home bank or card, and top up before your flight. On arrival, get a local SIM or eSIM so you have data at the counter, and keep a modest amount of riel for the genuinely offline corners of the country. Then do what everyone around you is doing: point your phone at the red code, check the name and the amount, and tap confirm. Cambodia without cash is not a stunt in 2026, it is simply how the country already pays.
